issues.description: The problem statement and UML explicitly require Farm to use a List (initialized as an ArrayList) to store animals and to provide getter/setter accordingly, but the solution implementation uses a Queue<Animal> with a LinkedList implementation and returns/accepts Queue in its getter/setter. This is a structural mismatch: the field type and constructor initialization differ from the specification and UML, which can confuse students about the expected collection type and API (e.g., using add vs offer) and violates the explicit instruction to initialize an ArrayList in the no-arg constructor.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the Farm implementation match the problem statement/UML: declare the animals field as List<Animal>, initialize it as a new ArrayList<>() in the no-argument constructor, and have the getter/setter use List<Animal>. Update addAnimal to use animals.add(a) and keep other methods iterating over the List. Alternatively, if Queue semantics are intended, update the problem statement and UML to specify Queue/LinkedList consistently.

issues.description: The problem statement requires the Farm to aggregate animals using a List and to initialize it with an ArrayList in the no-argument constructor, but the reference solution implements the collection as a Queue backed by a LinkedList (solution: Queue<Animal> animals = new LinkedList<>()). This mismatch in collection type identifiers (List/ArrayList vs Queue/LinkedList) creates a mapping confusion: students are instructed to use ArrayList in the task description but the provided final implementation uses different types, which may lead to unnecessary effort reconciling the required data structure with the example solution and ambiguity about the expected API for get/set/add operations.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the problem statement by changing the Farm collection type to List<Animal> and initializing it as new ArrayList<>() in the no-argument constructor (update getter/setter signatures to use List<Animal>). Alternatively, relax the problem text to permit any Collection implementation (e.g., Queue/LinkedList) so instructions match the provided solution.
